sections.history: Piranmalai is a hilly village in Singampunari taluk of Sivagangai district, and its hill temple is the Tirukkodunkundram of the Tevaram. It is counted among the fourteen Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Pandya country and was praised in a hymn by the child-saint Sambandar, while the later devotional poet Arunagiriar is also remembered as singing of the Lord of this hill. Local tradition recalls that the region was once called Parambu Nadu and the hill Parambu Malai, the name from which Piranmalai is said to have come, and the area is linked in popular memory with Paari, the generous chieftain counted among the seven great patrons. The age of the present structures and the dynasties who raised them are not firmly established in the sources we could consult, so the temple is best understood as a very old Tevaram-era sanctuary kept in worship by generation after generation of devotees.
sections.architecture: The temple is a hill sanctuary in the Dravidian tradition, set on a rocky hill said to rise more than two thousand feet above the surrounding country. The sanctum holds the Shiva linga of Kodunkundreesar, also called Kodunkundranathar, and the goddess Kuyilamudanayaki is honoured in her own shrine; the tamarind tree known locally as the Uranga Puli is the temple's sacred tree. The sacred water is the Madhu Pushkarini, also called the Thaenaazhi Theertham. On the hill are also a shrine of Vaduga Bhairavar, the shrine of Mangaibagar, and rock-cut spots known as the Pandava Therthams, while a dargah on the summit makes the hill a place of shared reverence for the local community. We have not found reliable measurements or a detailed description of the gopuram and mandapas, so none are given here.
sections.legends: The hill has its own origin story. In the sthala purana, the great serpent Adisesha coiled himself tightly around Mount Meru, and Vayu, the wind, blew with all his might to force him loose. In the fury of that wind, fragments of Meru were torn away and fell to earth, and one of them is remembered as this hill. The tale gives Piranmalai a kinship with the cosmic mountain and with the contest of strength between serpent and wind, and the hill is revered as a piece of the divine mountain itself. The name of the goddess, Kuyilamudanayaki, calls to mind the koel and nectar. We have kept to this central legend and have not repeated further local accounts that we could not confirm.
sections.festivals: The great annual festival is the Brahmotsavam in the Tamil month of Chithirai (April to May), when the deities are taken out in procession and the hill village fills with pilgrims. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Piranmalai asks for a patient and quiet visit. Approach the hill from the village and let the rock itself set your pace, for this is a temple of height and open sky rather than of crowded courtyards. Come first to the sanctum of Kodunkundreesar, then turn to the goddess Kuyilamudanayaki in her own shrine, and pause a moment at the Bhairavar and Mangaibagar shrines on the hill. Look out over the country below, and remember that this is a hill sung by Sambandar some thirteen centuries ago. Evenings are cooler, but the hill shrines close earlier than the main sanctum, so plan your ascent with the timings in mind.

visit.timings: The main sanctum is typically open from about 6:00 am to noon and again from about 4:00 pm to 8:00 pm; the Mangaibagar and Vaduga Bhairavar shrines close earlier in the evening, around 6:30 pm. Listings are older, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Piranmalai lies in Singampunari taluk of Sivagangai district, about 7 km from Singampunari, roughly 20 to 25 km from Tiruppathur and about 40 to 50 km from Karaikudi. Buses from Madurai to Ponnamaravathi pass through Piranmalai, and local buses run from Singampunari and Melur. Madurai is the nearest railway station and airport. Distances vary between sources, so confirm locally.
